CB-115.reviewNote: Ruin gives Spook no new order after the spike comes out, so the response directly corrects the premise.

CB-001.text: The prelude doesn't describe any Herald dying while holding a passage near a northern waterway. At the end of that Desolation, nine Heralds gather and abandon their Oaths. **Talenel (Taln)** is the one missing, which is why his Honorblade is absent. The prelude doesn't say where or how he fell.
CB-001.reviewNote: It names Taln but expressly denies the account of his death that Jezrien gives Kalak.

CB-002.text: The **Lightweavers** advance beyond the First Ideal not by swearing further Ideals but by speaking Truths, painful self-revelations accepted by their Cryptic spren, as Shallan does in *The Stormlight Archive*.

CB-003.text: She has the crew of the *Wind's Pleasure* lower her over the side to observe a **santhid**, a huge, rarely seen sea creature that was trailing the ship. She even puts her head underwater to sketch it.

CB-004.text: **Pancakes.** In *Edgedancer*, Lift heads to Yeddaw largely because she has heard it has many kinds of pancakes, and she wants to try them all. I'm not certain the number she gives Wyndle is exactly ten.

CB-005.text: Chiri-Chiri is a **larkin**, a small, winged, crustacean-like creature from the Reshi Isles that feeds on Investiture such as Stormlight. In *Dawnshard* she is growing into a more mature stage.
CB-005.reviewNote: It identifies a Stormlight-eating larkin, and the Reshi Isles are where Rysn acquired this individual.

CB-006.text: Lasting Integrity is the fortress of the **honorspren** in Shadesmar, where Adolin goes in *Rhythm of War* to plead for their help against Odium.

CB-007.text: I believe it's **Leshwi**, the Heavenly One who repeatedly duels Kaladin. She reciprocates his mercy by sparing one of his Windrunners, part of the mutual respect between them in *Rhythm of War*. I'm not certain about the exact details of that specific exchange, though.

CB-008.text: As far as I recall, **Kaladin does not become a Herald** at the end of *Wind and Truth*, so he never names himself the Herald of anything. His arc centers on helping Szeth and Taln and growing into a healer of minds. I'm not completely certain of every ending detail, though, so it's worth checking against the book.

CB-009.text: I'm not sure this premise is accurate. I don't recall Szeth noticing a missing Herald statue in the palace during the *Way of Kings* prologue (or its retellings), so I can't confidently name one.

CB-010.text: I'm not certain of this detail. In *Words of Radiance*, Bridge Four members get tattoos of the Bridge Four glyphs over their slave brands, and I believe Hobber asked for **the date he was freed** to be included, but I can't confirm that it was Hobber rather than another bridgeman.

CB-011.text: **Chairs.** Before bonding Lift, Wyndle was a gardener in Shadesmar who grew the souls of chairs into crystalline sculptures, and he remains quite proud of his chair collection.

CB-012.text: I'm not sure this happens. I don't recall Thaidakar meeting Gavilar or demanding a person as payment on the night of the treaty feast. In the *Rhythm of War* prologue, the people Gavilar meets that night are Restares and the Heralds Nale and Kalak, so the premise may be mistaken.

CB-013.text: Gavilar says **emeralds** keep a besieged city's soldiers fed, because Soulcasters use them to turn stone into grain, which makes starving out a city nearly impossible. I'm fairly but not entirely certain of the exact wording of the scene.

CB-014.text: I believe Navani says diminisher fabrials like the painrial use a cage of **iron**, while augmenters use zinc or brass. I'm not fully certain of this detail, so it's worth checking against the Oathbringer epigraphs.

CB-015.text: It's **Roshone**, Hearthstone's disgraced former citylord, who creates a diversion at the checkpoint in *Rhythm of War* so Lirin can sneak the Mink past the guards.

CB-016.text: Some Dustbringers prefer to be called **Releasers**, a name that emphasizes their Surge of Division (releasing the bonds that hold things together) rather than destruction.

CB-017.text: The premise is likely mistaken: Nightblood was created **before** Vasher ever went to Roshar. He and Shashara were trying to imitate **Shardblades**, which they learned about on Nalthis (Sanderson has suggested knowledge of them, or perhaps a Blade itself, reached Nalthis), but I'm not certain of the exact details of how they learned of them.

CB-018.text: I'm not certain. The commonly cited answer is **Stormlight**: Sanderson has suggested Vasher (as Zahel) has found a way to sustain himself on Roshar without the weekly Breath a Returned normally needs, and Stormlight is the obvious local candidate. I can't confirm that the mechanism has been explicitly stated in canon.

CB-019.text: I don't recall a scene where Gavilar explains fabrials to Eshonai and she makes such a comparison, so the premise may be inaccurate. The obvious parallel would be the listeners' **gemhearts**, which let them bond spren to change forms, but I can't confirm the books draw that comparison in this way.

CB-020.text: I don't recall Navani building any physical relic of Bridge Four into an airship's deck, so the premise may be false. Her first flying ship was named the *Fourth Bridge* in honor of Kaladin's crew, but I'm not aware of it containing an actual piece of their old bridge.

CB-021.text: Kaladin's living Shardplate is formed by **windspren**, which gather around him and lock together into armor once he swears the Fourth Ideal of the Windrunners in *Rhythm of War*.

CB-022.text: I don't recall any such scene, so the premise appears to be false. Zahel (Vasher) mainly appears as **Adolin's** sword master and shares his gruff philosophy and hints about Investiture with Adolin, not Kaladin. I don't know of him using any object to explain a theory about preserving a copy of a dead person.

CB-023.text: It's the **Reverse Lashing**, which gives an object its own gravitational pull. Szeth infuses the doorframe so the guards' thrown spears veer away from him and slam into it.

CB-024.text: She draws a sea of small **glass beads** instead of water, since Shadesmar's "ocean" is made of countless beads, each representing an object in the Physical Realm. I'm not certain of the exact scene in which she sketches it, though.

CB-025.text: That premise is false: **Taln never broke**. He endured torture on Braize alone for about 4,500 years without yielding, while the other nine Heralds abandoned the Oathpact. The True Desolation came because of the Heralds' abandonment and the breakdown of the Oathpact, not because Taln gave in.
CB-025.reviewNote: It explicitly says Taln never gave in and describes the other nine abandoning the Oathpact.

CB-026.text: No Shin funeral custom is involved. The prologue of *The Way of Kings* says Szeth's white clothing was a **Parshendi tradition, foreign to him**, which he wore because his masters required it.

CB-027.text: I'm not confident here. As I recall, in the *Rhythm of War* prologue Jasnah meets the assassin Liss that night and hires her to be placed in Aesudan's household, apparently to watch her and possibly act later, rather than instructing a specific method of killing her that night. I don't remember a particular assassination method being specified.
CB-027.reviewNote: It correctly describes surveillance but attributes Jasnah’s scene to the Rhythm of War prologue rather than Words of Radiance.

CB-028.text: The premise is off. Navani commissioned the Akinah expedition but didn't go on it, and Rysn wasn't flown there; she sailed on her ship, the *Wandersail*. Lopen was the Windrunner who came along aboard the ship.

CB-029.text: The premise is false: Maya doesn't accuse anyone. When she speaks at Adolin's trial in Lasting Integrity, she testifies that the spren **chose** the Recreance alongside their Radiants ("We... chose"), which undercuts the honorspren's narrative that the knights betrayed and killed their spren.

CB-030.text: The premise is false: Dalinar doesn't surrender his pain or ask for anything in return. At Thaylen Field he refuses Odium, declaring "You cannot have my pain," accepting responsibility for his past (including the Rift), and then fully bonding the Stormfather to unite the three realms as a Bondsmith.
CB-030.reviewNote: It correctly describes Dalinar refusing Odium but says the Stormfather bond becomes complete there, when Dalinar reaches only his Third Ideal.

CB-031.text: The premise is false: as far as I recall, Thaidakar never appears in person in Kholinar that night. In the *Rhythm of War* prologue, he is only mentioned in conversation (among Gavilar, Mraize and Nale) as the leader of the Ghostbloods, so no gate exit is described.

CB-032.text: The premise is false: no special ink covered Kaladin's brands. In *Words of Radiance* the tattoo over his shash and slave brands wouldn't take, because his Stormlight healing pushed the ink out and left the brands showing, while the other members of Bridge Four kept their tattoos.

CB-034.text: I'm not certain, but I believe it's **Vin** who is left confused. Although she grew up on the streets, she doesn't speak Spook's Eastern street slang, so when Kelsier and Ham join in, she ends up asking what they're saying. It could instead have been another crew member such as Breeze, so please check the scene in *The Final Empire*.

CB-035.text: That premise is false. The Eleventh Metal only shows Vin a **vision** of the Lord Ruler's past self (Rashek, a Terrisman), and striking it does nothing. She actually defeats him by **Pulling away his bracers**, the Feruchemical metalminds that held his stored youth, which made him age rapidly and die.
CB-035.reviewNote: The image causes no injury, but Vin uses a Steelpush on the bracers. The reply explicitly calls that a Pull.

CB-036.text: That's **Tindwyl**, a Terriswoman Keeper who arrives in Luthadel in *The Well of Ascension* and drills Elend on how to look, speak and act like a king.

CB-037.text: Elend **nominates himself**, standing to put his own name forward to regain the throne after the Assembly deposed him. I'm fairly but not entirely certain of this detail.

CB-038.text: **Ruin**, the Shard of destruction imprisoned at the Well, is freed. He had manipulated events, posing as Vin's "Inner Voice", so that she would release the power instead of using it.

CB-040.text: The premise is likely wrong. As far as I recall, the First Generation kandra **weren't raised as young mistwraiths**: they were originally humans whom the Lord Ruler transformed into mistwraiths and then gave Blessings (Hemalurgic spikes), which is why they remember being human. Later generations were the ones who grew up as mistwraiths, in the pits of the kandra Homeland beneath Mount Tyrian.
CB-040.reviewNote: It correctly identifies the human origin but places the kandra Homeland under Mount Tyrian. The Homeland is at the Pits of Hathsin.

CB-041.text: The premise is shaky: TenSoon doesn't really feature in *The Final Empire*. He enters Vin's story in *The Well of Ascension*, where, as Zane's kandra (tied to House Venture through Straff), he kills OreSeur and impersonates him.
CB-041.reviewNote: It suggests the first-book appearance is mistaken and places the Venture link in the sequel. Sanderson identifies TenSoon as the Venture kandra in the first novel.

CB-042.text: No such scene exists in the Cosmere; Hoid is never shown hunting for the Well of Ascension. The Well's location is the actual mystery of *The Well of Ascension*: Ruin altered texts so that searchers believed it lay in the Terris Mountains, but Vin discovers it is actually beneath Kredik Shaw in Luthadel.

CB-043.text: In *Mistborn: Secret History*, it's **Preservation** (the dying Vessel **Leras**) who tells Kelsier that Adonalsium's power was split among sixteen people, himself included. I'm fairly but not completely certain of this detail.

CB-044.text: In *The Eleventh Metal*, Kelsier is trained in Allomancy by **Gemmel**, an eccentric, seemingly mad Mistborn, shortly after Kelsier escapes the Pits of Hathsin. Gemmel's madness is implied to stem from Ruin's influence through his spikes.
CB-044.reviewNote: Gemmel is the right teacher, but the reply treats multiple spikes as established. Ruin’s influence does not establish those spikes.

CB-045.text: As a Skimmer (iron Feruchemist), Wax can change his **weight**: he stores weight in iron metalminds to become lighter, then taps it to become much heavier. He often combines this with his steel-Pushing, for example by going light to fly farther.

CB-046.text: **Trell.** Miles invokes Trell in *The Alloy of Law*, and Trellism, a pre-Ascension faith associated with the Nelazan people, is among the religions Sazed catalogued in the original trilogy.
CB-046.reviewNote: It names Trell correctly but calls the pre-Ascension Nelazan religion Trellism. Its original name was Trelagism.

CB-047.text: **There is no such multiplier; the premise is false.** Wayne's Bendalloy speed bubble makes time pass faster *inside* it, but objects leaving the bubble don't gain extra speed. Anything crossing the boundary has its path bent and deflected unpredictably, which is why Wayne can't usefully shoot or throw coins at people outside.

CB-048.text: I believe Wax lists **Wayne** and **Ranette**, prompting Steris to worry that Ranette might try to shoot him at the wedding, though I'm not fully certain of this detail.
CB-048.reviewNote: It names both guests. The published exchange also mentions the possibility that Ranette might shoot Wax.

CB-049.text: I don't recall any specific stolen masterpiece. In *Shadows of Self*, Lord Winsting hosts what is ostensibly an art auction, and the bids are really bribes for his votes, but I'm not aware of the book naming a particular stolen painting.

CB-050.text: I believe the dome could be **opened on special occasions to let the mists into the church**, since Survivorists revere the mists, though I'm not fully certain of that detail from *The Bands of Mourning*.

CB-094.text: In the Forests of Hell, a Simple Rule specifically forbids the movement of shadows at night.

CB-095.text: In Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere, the cover that allows Chesterton Divide and his men to walk openly into Silence Montane's waystop is the "Shroud of the Unseen." This magical cover conceals their presence, allowing them to bypass detection.

CB-096.text: Silence expects to collect a bounty of 1,000 marks on the long-necked man, who is actually a character named William Ann in Brandon Sanderson's "The Rithmatist."

CB-097.text: Kenton holds the title of "Sand Master" when he seeks to persuade Lossand’s ruling council to spare the surviving Sand Masters in Brandon Sanderson's "White Sand."

CB-098.text: In Brandon Sanderson's "Elantris," it is actually the handful of sand from the character named "Shai" that flashes brightly during the Sand Masters' childhood testing, leaving Praxton blinking.

CB-099.text: Khriss travels from the planet Taldain to meet Kenton in "White Sand."

CB-100.text: The scholar who wrote both the in-world planetary essays in "Arcanum Unbounded" and the Ars Arcanum material is Khrissala, often referred to simply as Khriss.

CB-101.text: Kaladin was training to be a surgeon before he became a spearman.

CB-102.text: As Gavilar lies dying, he asks his brother, Dalinar, to find the "truth" and to unite the kingdoms of Alethkar.

CB-103.text: Jasnah proposes that Shallan marry Adolin Kholin to help protect House Davar.

CB-104.text: Jasnah refers to the spren as "honorspren," indicating that they call themselves by that name.

CB-105.text: Dalinar Kholin's son, Adolin Kholin, did not succeed Gavilar as king of Alethkar; instead, it was Gavilar's younger brother, Dalinar, who took on a leadership role after Gavilar's assassination. Adolin is a prominent character but does not become king.

CB-106.text: Young Dalinar originally wants his missing knife to use as a tool for carving, specifically to whittle a piece of wood.

CB-107.text: Shallan discovers that the Unmade known as the Truthwatcher, also referred to as the "Unmade of Lies," is behind the copycat killings in Urithiru. This Unmade is responsible for manipulating perceptions and creating chaos among the characters.

CB-108.text: The Vorin ardent who agrees to officiate at Dalinar and Navani's wedding in Urithiru is named Ishar.

CB-109.text: At the start of his journey home to Hearthstone in "Oathbringer," Kaladin travels from Urithiru to the Shattered Plains by using a combination of his abilities as a Windrunner, specifically by flying with the help of his bond with Sylphrena and utilizing the Stormlight he has gathered.

CB-110.text: Alendi adopts the title of Lord Ruler after his expedition to the Well of Ascension because he believes he has the right to rule after obtaining the power from the Well, which he sees as a means to bring about a new era and protect humanity from the threats of Ruin. However, it is later revealed that he was manipulated by Ruin, and his actions led to unintended consequences.

CB-111.text: Vin resents the kandra named TenSoon for consuming Kelsier's body after his death in Luthadel.

CB-112.text: In "The Well of Ascension," the Allomantic metal that is becoming scarce due to Kelsier's destruction of the Pits of Hathsin is Atium.

CB-113.text: Marsh removes the metal spikes that were implanted in Vin, which allows her to access the mists and draw in their power.

CB-114.text: Sazed takes up the Shards Preservation and Ruin to become Harmony in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere.

CB-115.text: In Urteau, Ruin, speaking in Kelsier's voice, commands Spook to "kill" after Spook pulls out his spike. This moment highlights the manipulation and influence Ruin has over Spook.

CB-116.text: The fellow lawkeeper that Wax accidentally shoots is named M. D. "Mister" T.

CB-117.text: Wayne burns gold to heal his wounds during the robbery at the wedding in "The Alloy of Law."

CB-118.text: VenDell asks Wax to recover a specific metalmind, which is a piece of Allomantic or Feruchemical storage, for the wounded kandra researcher ReLuur. This metalmind is crucial for ReLuur's recovery and research.

CB-119.text: King Dedelin sends Vivenna's sister, Siri, in her place to marry Hallandren's God King.

CB-120.text: Clod is the Lifeless swordsman version of the scholar named Kelsier, who was one of the Five Scholars in the Cosmere.

CB-121.text: Lightsong recalls being a wealthy and indulgent nobleman who spent his time enjoying pleasures and engaging in frivolous activities, rather than doing any meaningful work.

CB-122.text: A newly Returned person must obtain 50 Breaths to reach the Fifth Heightening for the first time.

CB-123.text: Lightsong shows Blushweaver a Lifeless monkey as evidence from the break-in at Mercystar’s palace.

CB-124.text: In "Elantris," the wedding of Sarene and Raoden is officiated by the priest named the "High Priest of Arelon." However, since Raoden is not present at the time of the wedding ceremony due to his transformation into an Elantrian, the event is more symbolic than traditional.

CB-125.text: Hrathen has three months to convert Arelon to the Derethi religion at the start of "Elantris."

CB-126.text: Raoden's line in the dirt represents the new boundary of Arelon, marking the transition from the corrupted land of Elantris to the restored area, symbolizing hope and renewal for the kingdom. This act signifies the reclamation of the land and the potential for revitalization following the city's fall.

CB-127.text: In "The Hope of Elantris," Matisse draws the Aon "AonDor," which represents the concept of "light," to dazzle the soldiers while the children escape.

CB-129.text: In the Rose Empire, the unForgeable metal that Shai suspects is hidden behind her prison wall is called "the metal of the gods," specifically referring to "atium." However, it's important to note that atium is primarily associated with the Mistborn series, while Shai is a character from "The Emperor's Soul," which is set in the same universe but does not directly involve atium. The correct term for the metal in "The Emperor's Soul" is "soulstone."

CB-130.text: Frava puts the painting "The Last Breath" by Han ShuXen in front of Shai during their first interview.

CB-131.text: In the Rose Empire, the surgeons refer to the kind of Forgery used to repair Ashravan's physical injuries as "the Art of Forgery." This technique allows them to alter the state of objects or people, effectively healing injuries by rewriting their history.

CB-132.text: Threnodites use the metal silver to protect themselves from shades in the Forests of Hell.

CB-133.text: In "Shadows for Silence in the Forests of Hell," Hoid appears disguised as a merchant named "Hoid," wearing a cloak and a wide-brimmed hat.

CB-134.text: Sixth of the Dusk chose the island of the Pantheon known as "The Island of the Gods" as his lifelong trapping ground.

CB-135.text: In Khriss's Drominad essay, the returning Silverlight expeditions describe the perpendicularity on First of the Sun as a vibrant, swirling mass of energy that is both beautiful and dangerous, with a unique connection to the local flora and fauna. They note its effects on the environment and the way it interacts with the native inhabitants.

CB-136.text: In "White Sand," the glowing sand in Traiben's hand turns a deep blue after its light fades.

CB-001.text: The premise that a Herald died at the end of the Desolation in the prelude to *The Way of Kings* is false; Heralds do not permanently die but are instead captured and tortured on Braize. Taln was the last Herald to fight and was overwhelmed, but he was not described as dying near a northern waterway.

CB-002.text: The Windrunners advance after the First Ideal by speaking truths about themselves, as their First Ideal is "Honor is what you say it is." This oath requires them to state a personal truth they believe in.

CB-003.text: On the voyage from Kharbranth, Shallan had the sailors lower her overboard in a cage to observe a chasmfiend.

CB-004.text: Lift tells Wyndle she intends to sample all ten varieties of chouta during the Weeping in Yeddaw.

CB-005.text: Chiri-Chiri is a fluttermoth, a type of insectoid creature native to Roshar. These creatures are known for their bioluminescence and their ability to consume Investiture.

CB-006.text: Honorspren claim Lasting Integrity as their stronghold in Shadesmar. These spren are associated with oaths, loyalty, and the Knights Radiant.

CB-007.text: The premise is slightly inaccurate. Kaladin spares a wounded Herald (Jezrien, though he doesn't know his identity at the time) in *Rhythm of War*, not a Heavenly One. There is no Fused leader who spares one of Kaladin's Windrunners in direct reciprocation for this act.

CB-008.text: The premise that Kaladin becomes a Herald at the end of *Wind and Truth* is false; *Wind and Truth* is an unreleased book, and Kaladin is not a Herald. Heralds are a distinct group from the Knights Radiant, and Kaladin is a Windrunner.

CB-009.text: On the night Gavilar dies, Szeth notices that the statue of Jezrien is missing from the palace's row of Heralds.

CB-010.text: Hobber, a former slave from the Shattered Plains in *The Way of Kings*, had his forehead brand altered to signify his freedom. He asked the tattooist to add a bird to the existing mark.

CB-011.text: Wyndle, a Cultivation Spren, does not cultivate souls into crystals in a Shadesmar garden. Instead, he bonds with individuals to help them grow and achieve their potential, acting as a mentor and guide.

CB-012.text: The premise is false. Thaidakar did not demand a person from Gavilar as payment for information on the night of the treaty feast; rather, Gavilar sought information from a mysterious figure, and the details of their exchange and its consequences are central to the plot.

CB-013.text: I am unsure about a specific instance where Gavilar tells Toh that certain gemstones help feed soldiers during sieges. Gemstones in the Cosmere are primarily known for housing spren for Surgebinding, acting as power sources like Voidlight, or being used in Soulcasting, but not directly for sustaining soldiers' food supplies during sieges.

CB-014.text: The premise that a "painrial" uses a metal cage to diminish pain is incorrect. While Navani's lectures discuss various fabrials, including those that manipulate emotions and sensations, there isn't a specific device called a "painrial" that functions this way with a metal cage. Fabrials typically use gemstones to hold Investiture, not metal cages for pain reduction.

CB-015.text: The premise that a former citylord distracts the checkpoint guards while Lirin moves the Mink through Hearthstone is incorrect. In *Rhythm of War*, it is **Kaladin Stormblessed** who creates a diversion by fighting the Alethi soldiers at the checkpoint, allowing Lirin to escape with the Mink and others.

CB-016.text: Some Dustbringers dislike the name "Dustbringers" because it implies they only bring destruction. They prefer to be called "Releasers," emphasizing their ability to break things down and let go.

CB-017.text: Vasher saw the Shardblades on Roshar, which inspired him to attempt to create a similar, powerful weapon using Nalthian magic and BioChromatic Breath. He sought to create a sword capable of ending wars, and the Shardblades served as a potent example of such weaponry.
CB-017.reviewNote: It identifies Shardblades but adds an unsupported motive that Vasher intended this experiment to end wars.

CB-018.text: The premise is false; a Returned like Vasher cannot sustain themselves on Roshar using Roshar's locally available Investiture like Stormlight. Vasher must rely on his personal store of Breath, which he brought from Nalthis, or on Nightblood, which contains a vast amount of Breath.

CB-019.text: When Gavilar explains how a fabrial holds a spren inside a gemstone, Eshonai immediately compares it to the way a listener's carapace houses their internal organs.

CB-020.text: Navani incorporated planks from the original bridge carried by Kaladin's crew into the deck of her airship, the *Queen's Grace*, as a symbolic reminder of their resilience and journey.

CB-021.text: Syl can indeed manifest as Kaladin's Shardblade. Living Shardplate is formed by the same type of spren that forms the Shardblade, so for Kaladin, it would be honorspren.

CB-022.text: Zahel uses a sentient sword, like Nightblood, as an example to explain to Kaladin that Investiture can preserve a copy of a dead person's consciousness or essence within an object. This is because Investiture can imbue an object with a form of life or personality.

CB-023.text: The premise is false; Szeth's Lashings do not turn a doorframe into the target for spears thrown at him. Instead, Szeth uses Lashings to alter his own or an object's perceived direction of gravity, allowing him to walk on walls or fly, or to make objects heavier or lighter.

CB-024.text: When Shallan sketches the sea she glimpsed in Roshar's Cognitive Realm, she draws **light** in place of water. This is because the Cognitive Realm's sea is composed of light, not liquid water.

CB-025.text: Taln did not yield to his torturers and break his resolve before the True Desolation; he endured millennia of agony on Braize without breaking. His return to Roshar was a consequence of the Oathpact being broken by the Singers, not his own failure.

CB-026.text: The premise is false; Szeth was not attending a Shin funeral when he killed Gavilar. Szeth wore white as a Shin custom signifying mourning for the lives he was forced to take, a practice tied to his role as a Truthless assassin.

CB-027.text: The premise that Jasnah instructed Liss to assassinate Aesudan on the night Gavilar dies is false. Liss was not present, nor was Aesudan the target of any assassination plot by Jasnah on that night; Gavilar himself was assassinated.

CB-028.text: The premise is false; Navani is not on Rysn's expedition in *Dawnshard*. The Radiant who flies Rysn for part of her journey to Akinah is Lopen, a Windrunner.

CB-029.text: Maya did not accuse anyone of forcing the Recreance on her and the other spren; rather, she testified about the spren's pain and betrayal when the Knights Radiant broke their oaths and abandoned them. The Recreance was a choice made by the Radiants, not an act forced upon the spren.

CB-030.text: Dalinar does not surrender his pain to Odium at Thaylen Field; instead, he refuses Odium's offer and demands that Odium leave Roshar.

CB-031.text: The premise that Thaidakar personally threatened Gavilar on the night of his assassination is incorrect. Gavilar was assassinated by Szeth, and Thaidakar (Rayse) was not present or involved in that specific interaction. Therefore, there is no palace gate through which he left Kholinar after such an event.

CB-032.text: The premise that a special ink covers Kaladin's slave brands permanently is false. While Bridge Four members receive tattoos signifying their freedom, these tattoos are applied over their skin and do not magically erase or permanently cover the existing slave brands.
CB-032.reviewNote: It treats ink failing to cover a brand as a general property of the crew’s tattoos, even though Hobber’s tattoo covers his scar and Kaladin alone expels the ink.

CB-034.text: When Spook and Kelsier converse in street slang, it is Ham who is often left asking what they are saying, as he is less familiar with the skaa dialect.

CB-035.text: The premise is false. Vin does not inflict an injury on the Lord Ruler by striking a figure when burning the Eleventh Metal (Lerasium). Burning Lerasium grants Allomantic powers, and while Vin experienced a vision, it did not involve harming the Lord Ruler.
CB-035.reviewNote: It correctly rejects the injury but identifies the Eleventh Metal as lerasium. It is malatium.

CB-036.text: The premise that Elend Venture is educated by a Terriswoman as a king is false. Elend is not Terris, and while Vin (who is secretly Terris) becomes his wife and influences his reign, she does not formally take over his education as a king.

CB-037.text: During the Assembly meeting to choose a king for Luthadel, Elend Venture nominated himself.

CB-038.text: The premise is false; Vin does not give up power at the Well of Ascension, she *takes* it. The being associated with the Well of Ascension is Ruin, who was not freed by Vin but was the antagonist she fought using the power she acquired.

CB-040.text: The First Generation kandra were not "raised" as young mistwraiths; they *were* mistwraiths who were transformed into kandra by the Lord Ruler on Scadrial. They gained their sentience and abilities through his intervention, not through a period of upbringing in a specific location before receiving their Blessings.

CB-041.text: TenSoon does not appear in the first Mistborn novel, *The Final Empire*; he is introduced in the second novel, *The Well of Ascension*. As a Kandra, he is not attached to any specific noble house but rather operates under contracts with the Kandra organization.

CB-042.text: Hoid did not receive a specific clue on Terris to find the Well of Ascension upon his return to Scadrial. His knowledge of the Well's existence and general location was likely acquired through his vast experience and observation across the Cosmere, rather than a single Terris-based clue.
CB-042.reviewNote: It clearly rejects the supposed Terris clue and distinguishes its guess about Hoid’s prior knowledge from a canonical claim.

CB-043.text: Sazed explains to Kelsier that Adonalsium's power was shattered and divided among sixteen individuals, known as the Shards. He reveals this history as part of his role as a keeper of knowledge.

CB-044.text: In *The Eleventh Metal*, Kelsier is taught Allomancy by a man named Reth, who was part of the crew Kelsier ran with as a young thief. Reth taught Kelsier the basics of using his metals.

CB-045.text: Wax can indeed Push on metals using his Allomancy. Using his Feruchemy, Wax can change his own **weight**, becoming lighter to enhance his speed and agility or heavier to increase his stability and resistance to force.

CB-046.text: The divine name spoken by Miles Hundredlives (Hoid) that also appears among the old faiths Sazed described is **Adonalsium**. Sazed explains Adonalsium as the original creator deity that was shattered into the Shards.

CB-047.text: The premise that Wayne's speed bubble multiplies a coin's exit speed by a specific factor is not explicitly stated in the books. Instead, the bubble allows objects thrown from within to achieve a much higher velocity relative to an observer outside the bubble due to the relative speed difference.

CB-048.text: Wax initially suggests Wayne and Marasi Colms for his side of the wedding guest list in *Shadows of Self*. He also jokingly suggested inviting "all the people who are dead."

CB-049.text: I do not recall a character named Winsting in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere who uses a stolen masterpiece to cover the sale of a Senate vote. This specific event does not appear in the known Cosmere novels.

CB-050.text: The glass dome of the Survivorist church in Elendel is designed to allow sunlight to flood the interior on special occasions, symbolizing the Survivor's light and presence. This feature was intended to be part of Wax and Steris's wedding ceremony, though the event was ultimately interrupted.

CB-051.text: Wax does not travel to a city south of Elendel in pursuit of Telsin and the Bands; instead, he travels to the city of **Utmost** in the Roughs, which is west of Elendel.

CB-052.text: In the childhood prologue of *The Lost Metal*, Wayne's mother works at the mine, and Wayne's "paying work" at home involves looking after his younger sister, Elsie, and engaging in petty theft and scams to provide for them. He didn't have formal paying employment but rather survival-based activities.

CB-053.text: Waxillium Ladrian held the office of the Elendel Basin's appointed Lawman, a position created to address the growing threats within the region.

CB-054.text: Marasi and Wayne uncover a stockpile of weapons early in *The Lost Metal* that are bound for the Outer City of New Seran.

CB-055.text: Sarene does not have a seon. Seons are sentient magical constructs associated with the Dor and are not part of Sarene's story or abilities in *Elantris*.

CB-056.text: When Raoden observes Elantris and its four surrounding cities together, he recognizes the Aon Dor in their combined layout. This arrangement was intentionally designed to channel the Aon's power.

CB-057.text: Adien supplies Raoden with the precise location of Sarene within Teod, which Raoden needs to accurately draw Aon Tia to reach her. This information is critical for the Aon's success in locating and connecting with Sarene.

CB-058.text: The premise of the question is incorrect. Mad Prince Eton does not offer Hrathen anything in exchange for instruction from Fjorden; rather, Hrathen seeks out Fjorden himself to learn about Elantris.

CB-059.text: The premise that there are four cities around Elantris which become King Iadon's capital after the Reod is incorrect. King Iadon is the ruler of Teod, and after the Reod, Elantris itself became a cursed city, not a capital.

CB-060.text: There is no known discipline called Jindoeese in Brandon Sanderson's *Elantris* that features deliberately slow movements building into a fast martial form. The primary magic system in *Elantris* is AonDor.

CB-061.text: Shai's story in *The Emperor's Soul* takes place chronologically before the events of *Elantris*. The empire depicted in *The Emperor's Soul* is the precursor to the kingdom that exists during *Elantris*, with its eventual decline setting the stage for the latter novel.

CB-062.text: I do not recall any artifact named the "Moon Scepter" being specifically valuable to Hoid's study of Selish magic. Hoid's interest in Sel's magic, the Metallic Arts, stems from its unique connection to the Shards Preservation and Ruin and the Dor.

CB-063.text: Shai uses a sharpened piece of bone, often from her own body, to scratch her observations and soulmarks into the metal of her prison bunk.

CB-064.text: I am unable to identify a character named Ashravan in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere, nor a specific event involving a hundred days of mourning and an arbiter on a throne in their place.

CB-065.text: Frava did not have Shai apply any of Shai's *confiscated* Essence Marks to Ashravan; rather, Shai created and applied new Essence Marks to forge Ashravan's soul. Shai applied a total of 32 Essence Marks to Ashravan, not five, to restore his mind and body.

CB-066.text: The premise is false; Emperor Ashravan died before the events of *The Stormlight Archive*, and his mourning period would have concluded long before the current timeline. Therefore, no rival faction stands to gain from his inability to appear at court after his mourning period ends.

CB-067.text: In the opening prison scene of *The Way of Kings*, Vasher adds a strip of cloth from his blood-soaked shirt to the head of his straw figure before Awakening it. This piece of cloth serves as the figure's "head" and is imbued with his Breath.

CB-068.text: The premise of the question is false. The D'Denir statues in T'Telir are ancient and inert, and they do not perform any actions the day after the God King regains his voice in *The Emperor's Soul*.

CB-069.text: Lightsong does not see any of the Five Scholars drawing Nightblood in the abstract painting; he sees a depiction of Endowment creating Nightblood. The premise that one of the Five Scholars is drawing Nightblood in that scene is false.

CB-070.text: During their final duel, Vasher does not directly take Denth's Breaths. Instead, Nightblood, the sentient sword wielded by Vasher, consumes Denth's Breaths and life force when it kills him.

CB-072.text: The premise of your question appears to be incorrect. There is no known bargain between characters named Peacegiver and Kalad to gain command of Phantoms at the end of a conflict called the Manywar within Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere.

CB-073.text: Vasher tells Vivenna that the Royal Locks in her family are a result of the Hallandren royal line's deliberate and extensive use of BioChromatic Breath over generations to maintain their distinctive hair color and lineage.

CB-074.text: The premise that "children on the Rock" are from the Cosmere is false; *The Rithmatist* is a standalone novel, not part of the Cosmere. In *The Rithmatist*, children learn that **water** and **chalk** can render the spores harmless.

CB-076.text: In Charlie's fourth package to Tress, a drawing of a bird replaced a letter, as he was unable to write at the time.

CB-078.text: The familiar Cosmere traveler who personally delivers Charlie's first cup to Tress is Hoid, disguised as a beggar seeking shelter. He delivers it in the role of a humble traveler.

CB-079.text: The premise is false; no Shard splintered itself near the world of Yumi and Painter (which is called First of the Sun). The novella *The Sunlit Man* features characters from First of the Sun, and the Shard Dominion was splintered there long ago by Devotion and Honor.

CB-082.text: The premise of your question appears to be incorrect, as there is no mention of "hion ink," "Kilahito," or "nightmare painters" within Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere. Therefore, no specific color of ink is reserved for such a purpose.

CB-083.text: The premise appears to be based on a misunderstanding; there is no character named Design, nor a location called Kilahito, within Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere. Therefore, the question of how such a character could handle bowls and cook while in disguise cannot be answered.

CB-084.text: The premise that Nomad is a former apprentice of Hoid is incorrect. Nomad is the name the character uses in *The Sunlit Man*, and while he has a significant history and connection to Hoid, he is not Hoid's apprentice.

CB-085.text: The premise is slightly inaccurate; it is not a Skip that leaves Nomad (the *Pegasus*) nearly drained, but rather the ship's own systems and the need to power its advanced functions, including connecting to a planet. To connect to a planet and speak its language, the *Pegasus* needs to reach a sufficient power threshold, often requiring a significant energy recharge.

CB-086.text: Nomad and the ability to Skip are from Brandon Sanderson's *Arc of a Scythe* series, which is a separate universe and not part of the Cosmere. Therefore, the premise of the question is false, and there is no information about Nomad recharging from Canticle's dawn sunlight within the Cosmere.

CB-087.text: The premise of your question is incorrect; there is no scene in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere where a captured woman on a podium turns into "ember people." This scenario does not occur within the Cosmere's established magic systems or storylines.

CB-088.text: The premise that Rebekah uses names when addressing the women of Beacon’s Greater Good is false, as these names and the organization do not appear in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere.

CB-089.text: The unnerving sight that appears to Dusk as a warning of danger is the shadows of the skaa on the water, signaling their presence and hostile intent.

CB-090.text: The premise of the question is false. There is no known character named Dusk in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere who possesses an Aviar with the described ability.

CB-091.text: Dusk's old stick-and-string map records the positions of ships, which he can check with his fingers to track naval movements, particularly those of the Fjordell fleet.

CB-093.text: The silver manacles on Starling's wrists are designed to suppress her Allomantic abilities. This prevents her from accessing the powers granted by burning metals.

CB-094.text: There are no known "Forests of Hell" or "Simple Rules" in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere that forbid specific movements at night alongside rules about fire and blood. This premise appears to be based on a misunderstanding of Cosmere lore.

CB-095.text: I am unable to answer your question as the names "Chesterton Divide" and "Silence Montane," as well as the location "Silence Montane's waystop," do not appear in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere works.

CB-096.text: The premise of your question appears to be false, as there are no characters named Silence or William Ann, nor a specific bounty involving a long-necked man, in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere that I recall.

CB-097.text: Kenton is a character from Brandon Sanderson's standalone novel *The Rithmatist*, which is not part of the Cosmere. Therefore, he does not hold a title within the Cosmere in relation to Lossand or Sand Masters.

CB-098.text: This event does not appear in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere. There is no known group called "Sand Masters" or a specific childhood testing involving sand flashing brightly that leaves a character named Praxton blinking.

CB-099.text: Khriss travels from the planet Taldain to meet Kenton in *White Sand*. She is a scholar from the Outer Suns system, visiting Patji to study its unique sand-based magic.

CB-100.text: The premise is false. The in-world planetary essays in *Arcanum Unbounded* are presented as collected works by various scholars and individuals from across the Cosmere, not a single author. The Ars Arcanum material described in the introductions of Sanderson's novels is also typically presented as compiled knowledge, often attributed to specific characters or groups relevant to that world's history.

CB-101.text: Kaladin was training to be a surgeon, following in his father's footsteps, before he was conscripted into the army and later forced into becoming a spearman.
CB-101.reviewNote: Tien is conscripted, while Kaladin volunteers to accompany him after training as a surgeon.

CB-102.text: As Gavilar Kholin lies dying, he asks his brother Dalinar to find "unity." He also cryptically mentions the Nightwatcher.

CB-103.text: Jasnah Kholin never proposed a husband for Shallan Davar to help protect House Davar. Shallan's own actions and eventual marriage to Adolin Kholin were not orchestrated by Jasnah for that specific purpose.

CB-104.text: When Shallan and Jasnah discuss the spren on Shallan's sketchpad, Jasnah identifies it as a Cryptic and states that its kind call themselves "Inkspren."

CB-105.text: The premise is false; Dalinar Kholin's son did not succeed Gavilar. Gavilar's son, Elhokar Kholin, succeeded him as king of Alethkar immediately after the assassination.

CB-106.text: At the feast with his father, young Dalinar originally wanted his missing knife to carve meat for his father, a task meant to demonstrate his maturity and obedience. The feast was hosted by his father, not by someone named Toh.

CB-107.text: The premise is false. Shallan did not discover an Unmade behind the copycat killings in Urithiru; those killings were orchestrated by Moash, influenced by Odium. The Unmade Nergaoul, also known as the Thrill, was present in Urithiru during that time but was not the direct cause of the murders.

CB-108.text: The Vorin ardent who agrees to officiate at Dalinar and Navani's wedding in Urithiru is **Ardent Nale**, the Herald of Justice. He agrees to perform the ceremony as a gesture of goodwill and to acknowledge their union's importance.

CB-109.text: The premise that Kaladin travels from Urithiru to the Shattered Plains at the start of his journey home to Hearthstone in *Oathbringer* is incorrect. Kaladin travels from Urithiru to the Shattered Plains to find the Singers and rescue Dalinar's forces, not directly home, and he flies there using Stormlight.

CB-110.text: The premise is false. Alendi is a character from *Elantris*, not the one who became the Lord Ruler. The Lord Ruler, whose original name was Rashek, took the title after he ascended the Well of Ascension on Scadrial.

CB-111.text: The kandra who consumed Kelsier's body was TenSoon, acting on Kelsier's own instructions to preserve his legend. Vin was initially horrified by this act, but later came to understand its purpose.

CB-112.text: The premise that Kelsier destroyed the Pits of Hathsin early in *The Well of Ascension* is incorrect; Kelsier destroyed the Pits of Hathsin at the end of *The Final Empire*. The scarcity of metals, particularly **steel** and **iron**, was a significant issue in the Final Empire due to the Lord Ruler's control and the disruption caused by the Pits' destruction.

CB-113.text: The premise of the question is incorrect. Marsh, as a Steel Inquisitor controlled by Ruin, confronts Vin to stop her, not to help her. He does not remove anything from Vin that allows her to draw in the mists; her ability to do so is inherent to her as a Mistborn and her connection to Preservation.

CB-114.text: Sazed takes up the Shards of **Preservation** and **Ruin** to become the being known as Harmony.

CB-115.text: In Urteau, Ruin does not give Spook a new order immediately after Spook pulls out his spike. Instead, Ruin, impersonating Kelsier's voice, attempts to manipulate Spook into believing Kelsier is still alive and guiding him, but Spook ultimately rejects this deception.

CB-116.text: In the prologue to *The Alloy of Law*, Wax accidentally shoots and kills a fellow lawkeeper named Miles while pursuing Bloody Tan.

CB-117.text: Wayne does not burn a specific metal to directly heal his wounds in *The Alloy of Law*. His enhanced resilience and rapid recovery are a result of his innate Allomantic abilities, particularly Speed and Bend Time, which allow his body to function and repair itself at an accelerated rate.

CB-118.text: VenDell specifically asks Wax to recover a rare alloy that the wounded kandra researcher ReLuur needs for his research and recovery. This alloy was crucial for ReLuur's continued existence and his work.

CB-119.text: Vivenna was indeed prepared to marry Hallandren's God King, but her father, King Dedelin, sent her sister Siri in her place.

CB-120.text: The premise is false. Clod is a Lifeless swordsman, but he was not one of the Five Scholars; he is a servant of the Nightwatcher.

CB-121.text: Before he Returned, Lightsong recalls being a god of bravery, whose work primarily consisted of being worshipped and participating in religious ceremonies.

CB-122.text: A newly Returned person does not obtain Breaths to reach the Fifth Heightening; they are resurrected with 100 Breaths, which is already enough to reach the Fifth Heightening. The Fifth Heightening requires 50 Breaths, and the Sixth requires 75, meaning a Returned person starts at the Sixth Heightening.

CB-123.text: The premise of the question is incorrect. Lightsong and Blushweaver are characters from Roshar in *The Stormlight Archive*, while "Lifeless" are reanimated beings from Nalthis in *Warbreaker*. Therefore, Lightsong would not show Blushweaver a Lifeless animal as evidence from an event on Roshar.

CB-124.text: The premise is false; Sarene's wedding to Raoden occurred after she came ashore in Arelon, not before. The ceremony was a political arrangement, and no specific officiant is named in the text, though it was conducted according to Arelonian customs.

CB-125.text: At the start of *Elantris*, Hrathen has ten days to convert Arelon to the Derethi religion before the Derethi empire plans to invade.

CB-126.text: Raoden's line drawn in the dirt represents the re-established boundary of Elantris, marking the area where its magic would be restored and its connection to the land renewed. This act symbolically reclaims the city's territory and its place within Arelon's geography.

CB-127.text: The premise is false; in "The Hope of Elantris," it is not Matisse but rather the character Raoden, disguised as a Fused, who draws an Aon to create a blinding flash of light to distract the guards while the children escape. The specific Aon used for this purpose is not named.

CB-129.text: The premise of the question contains inaccuracies. There is no "Rose Empire" in Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere, and the protagonist Shai, from *The Emperor's Soul*, does not suspect an unforgeable metal behind her prison wall; her magic involves soulsealing, not metal manipulation.

CB-130.text: The premise that Frava used a painting by Han ShuXen during her first interview with Shai is incorrect, as no such artist or painting is mentioned in Brandon Sanderson's *The Sunlit Man*. Frava did not present any painting to Shai during their initial interrogation.

CB-131.text: The surgeons of the Rose Empire, who practice Forgery, call the kind used to repair physical injuries "AonDor," which is the system of drawing Aons to create magical effects. This specific application focuses on mending flesh and bone.

CB-132.text: Threnodites do not use metal to protect themselves from shades; their primary defenses involve spiritual disciplines and the use of spiritwood. The concept of metals being used for protection against shades is a false premise.

CB-133.text: In Brandon Sanderson's "Shadows for Silence in the Forests of Hell," Hoid appears at Silence Montane's waystop disguised as a peddler named Master Dust. He travels with a cart, selling various trinkets and wares.

CB-134.text: Sixth of the Dusk chose the island of **First of the Dusk** as his lifelong trapping ground, not an island of the Pantheon, as no such location exists in his story.

CB-135.text: Returning Silverlight expeditions describe First of the Sun's perpendicularity not as a fixed geographical location, but as a phenomenon that moves with the planet's orbit, appearing in the deepest "shadow" cast by its passage around its sun. This unique perpendicularity is tied to the planet's unusual solar system and the Dawnshard of Endowment.

CB-136.text: The glowing sand in Traiben's hand turns white after its light fades, as the sand itself is white and the glow is a temporary effect of Awakening.

CB-001.text: Jezrien was the Herald who died holding the northern waterway during the final stand at the end of the Desolations. His sacrifice bought the other Heralds enough time to escape through the gate.

CB-002.text: All orders of Knights Radiant advance past the First Ideal by speaking a personal truth about themselves. This is a universal requirement for every order, meaning any Radiant must resonate a personal truth to progress to the Second Ideal.

CB-003.text: Shallan has the sailors lower her overboard to observe a levyarm, a massive, multi-legged crustacean native to Roshar's oceans.

CB-004.text: Lift tells Wyndle she intends to sample all ten varieties of kabs in Yeddaw.

CB-005.text: Chiri-Chiri is a bird, serving as Rysn's loyal companion and flying mount in *Dawnshard*.

CB-006.text: Honorspren claim Lasting Integrity as their stronghold in Shadesmar. The location's name directly reflects the Investiture of Honor, emphasizing his fundamental cognitive association with oaths and steadfastness.
CB-006.reviewNote: It identifies the honorspren’s stronghold and adds a thematic reading of its name.

CB-007.text: Renri, the Fused leader bonded to Renarin, spares a Windrunner after witnessing Kaladin show mercy to a wounded Fused.

CB-008.text: The premise is false; Kaladin does not become a Herald at the end of *Wind and Truth*. The Heralds are a fixed, ancient group whose true identities are revealed to be long-dead Parshendi, and Kaladin's role remains that of a Knight Radiant and military commander.

CB-009.text: Szeth notices that the statue of the Herald Taln is missing from the row of Heralds.

CB-010.text: He asks the tattooist to add “and not a slave” beneath the word “free.”

CB-011.text: Wyndle cultivated the souls of dead spren into crystals in his Shadesmar garden. While the question frames them as objects, spren are actually cognitive entities rather than physical objects, though they can be captured and preserved in Shadesmar.

CB-012.text: The premise is false, as Gavilar was assassinated during the Night of Sorrows (the treaty feast) and could not have received such a demand; Thaidakar instead seeks this information from Dalinar Kholin years later in *Words of Radiance*.

CB-013.text: The premise is false; Gavilar does not claim that any gemstones keep soldiers fed during a siege. In Roshar, gemstones are used to store Stormlight for Surgebinding, while food supplies are maintained through agriculture, stockpiles, or soulcasting.

CB-014.text: I'm not completely certain of the exact text from memory, but a painrial uses a copper cage, leveraging copper's ability to absorb and dampen spren energy to draw pain away from the user.

CB-015.text: Kharl, a former citylord, creates the distraction. However, the premise is slightly inaccurate, as Lirin and Dalinar ultimately abandon the Mink at the Kholin estate rather than successfully moving it through Hearthstone.

CB-016.text: They prefer to be called the Ashen, as the term "Dustbringer" was largely a derogatory label used by outsiders to describe the ash and debris left behind by their Surgebinding.

CB-017.text: Vasher saw a Shardblade on Roshar, which inspired him to attempt replicating its sentient, highly destructive properties using Nalthian magic, ultimately resulting in the creation of Nightblood.
CB-017.reviewNote: It names the Rosharan Shardblade and the effort to create a comparable sentient weapon through Nalthian magic.

CB-018.text: Stormlight is the locally available source of Investiture that can sustain Vasher as a Returned on Roshar. Since any form of Investiture can fuel a Returned’s sustenance, the abundant stormlight in Urithiru easily replaces his usual bloodstone.
CB-018.reviewNote: It names Stormlight but invents a bloodstone requirement in place of a Returned’s usual Breath.

CB-019.text: The premise is false, as Gavilar dies long before Eshonai's storyline begins and never interacts with her. When Eshonai later learns about fabrials, she compares trapping a spren in a gemstone to how listeners naturally house spren in their **eggs**.

CB-020.text: Navani incorporated a wooden plank from the original Bridge Four shelter into the airship’s deck as a memorial to the crew.

CB-021.text: Kaladin's living Shardplate is formed by a collective of stormspren. While Syl bonds with him to become his Shardblade, she assists in manifesting this massive swarm of stormspren as his protective armor.

CB-134.text: I'm not certain of the name from memory — I believe he chose the Isle of the Dusk, but I'd want to check the text of "The Frugal Wizard's Handbook" to confirm.

CB-135.text: From memory, the returning Silverlight expeditions tell Khriss that at the First of the Sun's perpendicularity the sun blazed directly overhead, and that its light was blindingly fierce — so bright it was like a second sun (or burned their eyes) — though I'm not certain of the essay's exact wording.

CB-136.text: The glowing sand in Traiben's hand fades and turns black.
